translations.text: "When the days of Mary's purification were fulfilled," and so on.
In the old law God commanded, and ordered Moses the leader to write it down among the other commandments, that every woman who bore a child should wait forty days after the birth,
so that she should not come into God's temple, nor into one bed with her husband, before the time we have just mentioned, that is, forty days, if it was a boy-child.
But if it was a girl-child, then she had to keep away from entering God's house for eighty days, and also from her bedfellow.

After that time she was to go to God's house with an offering, and bring the child forth with the offering, and afterwards, with God's blessing, go to her husband again. This was laid down concerning women.
Now the holy maiden Mary, Christ's mother, was nevertheless mindful of God's commandments, and on this day she went to God's house with an offering,
and brought the child she had borne, the Saviour Christ, presented as an offering to God's temple, just as it was laid down in God's law.
There was then in the city of Jerusalem a man of God, and his name was Simeon.
He was very righteous and had great fear of God, and he was waiting for the comfort that had been promised to the people of Israel, that is, the coming of Christ.
The Holy Spirit dwelt in this Simeon, and he knew well enough that the Almighty Son of God would come to men and take on human nature.
This man greatly longed for the Saviour's coming, and every day in his prayers he begged God that he might see Christ before he tasted death.
Then, because he had so great a longing for Christ's coming, an answer came to him from the Holy Spirit, that he would not taste death before he had seen Christ.
He was then glad of the promise, and came to God's temple at the prompting of the Holy Spirit.
Then the holy Mary came to the temple with the child, and the old man Simeon went to meet the child. He saw the Saviour and knew him well, that he was the Son of God, the Redeemer of the whole world.
He then took him in his arms with great fervour, carried him into the temple, and earnestly thanked God that he had been allowed to see him.
Then he said, "My Lord, now you let me depart from this life in peace, according to your word,
because my eyes have seen your Saviour, whom you have prepared before the face of all people: a light for revelation to the nations, and glory for your people Israel."
It is written in Christ's book, and in other books as well, that many prophets and righteous men wished to see Christ's coming, but it was not granted to them. It was granted to this old man,
because it is written of him that he said every day in his prayers, "Oh, when will the Saviour come?
When will he be born? When may I see him? Will I be allowed to live until I see him?"
Because of this longing an answer came to him, that he would not see death before he had seen Christ.
Mary, Christ's mother, carried the child, and the old Simeon went to meet her. He recognised the child through revelation, embraced it and carried it into the temple.
He carried the child, and the child carried him. How did the child carry him? The old Simeon carried in his arms the one who holds and governs all things.
He appeared small there, yet he was nevertheless very great and immeasurable. He appeared small because he wished to fetch the small ones and bring them up to his kingdom.
Who are the small ones whom he wished to have up in his kingdom? They are the humble.
Christ did not seek the proud, those who are great in their own thoughts; but those who are small and humble in their hearts come to God's kingdom. No pride may climb up there.

The devil was there and grew proud, but his pride cast him down into the depths of hell. Therefore our frailty cannot climb up there if it is proud, since the angel could not remain there once he grew proud.
God commanded his people in the old law that they should offer him every firstborn male child, or else redeem it with five shillings.
Also among their cattle, whatever was firstborn they were to bring to God's house and offer it there to God.
If it was an unclean beast, then the owner had to kill it, or give God another, clean beast instead. We need not keep these commandments bodily now, but spiritually.
When some good thing is born in our mind and we turn it into deeds, then we must credit it to God's grace and commit it to God.
We must redeem our evil thoughts or deeds with five shillings; that is, we must repent of our wickedness with our five senses, which are sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.
Likewise, the unclean beasts signify our unclean thoughts and deeds, which we must always kill, or exchange for clean ones;
that is, we must always quench our uncleanness and our wickedness, and forsake evil and do good.
Then the blessed Mary offered her gift to God with the child, as it was laid down in God's law.
It was laid down in the old law by God's command that those who could afford it were to bring a year-old lamb with their child as an offering to God, and a dove or a turtle-dove.
If, however, any woman were so poor that she could not obtain these things, then she was to bring two young pigeons, or two turtledoves.
The lesser offering, that is, the birds, which was the offering of poor people, was offered for Christ. The Almighty Son of God was very mindful of our needs in all things;
not only did he wish to become man for us, though he was God, but he also wished to be poor for us, though he was rich,
so that he might give us a share in his kingdom and fellowship in his divinity. The lamb signifies innocence and the greater goodness;
If, then, we are so poor that we cannot offer the greater good to God, then we must bring him two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, that is, a twofold compunction, of fear and of love.
A person is moved to compunction in two ways: first he fears the torment of hell and weeps for his sins; afterwards he comes to love God;
then he begins to lament, and it seems too long to him until he is taken from the hardships of this life and brought to eternal rest.
A lamb, or two turtle-doves, was a small thing to bring to God; but he does not look so much at a person's offering as he looks at his heart.
God has no need of our possessions; all things are his, heaven and earth and sea, and all the things that dwell in them;

but he gave earthly things to people for their use, and commanded them to acknowledge him, who had given them those earthly things, with those same things, not for his need but for the need of mankind.
If you acknowledge your Lord with your possessions, according to your means, it benefits you yourself toward eternal life;
If you forget him, it harms yourself and not God, and you will lose the eternal reward. God desires the goodness of your mind, and not your possessions.
If you do anything in praise of God with a generous mind, then you show the goodness of your mind by that deed;
If, however, you will do no good to the honour of God, then by that vice you reveal your wickedness, and that wickedness will destroy you before God.
In the old law it is set down everywhere that God frequently commanded these birds to be offered as his offering, because of the meaning that they signify.
Now no one is permitted to keep the old law bodily, but let everyone keep it spiritually.
Doves are very harmless and gentle birds, and they love unity, and they fly in flocks.
Let the Christian man do likewise: let him be harmless and gentle, and love unity and brotherhood among Christian people; then he spiritually offers the young doves to God.
The turtledoves signify chastity: they are so made that if one of them loses the other, the living one never seeks another mate.
If, then, the Christian man does so for the love of God, then he offers the turtledoves in the best way.
These two kinds of bird do not sing as other birds do; instead they moan, because they signify the moaning of holy people in this life, just as Christ said to his apostles,
"You will be made sad in this life, but your sadness will be turned to everlasting joy." And again he said, "Blessed are those who weep for their sins, for they will be comforted."
The old man Simeon, of whom we spoke before, did not desire that he might hear Christ speak, because he knew that he was God, even though he was still unable to speak in his human nature.
He could have spoken if he had wished; and he was just as wise then, when he was one night old, as he was when he was thirty years old;
but he wished to wait for the time of his growth in his human nature, as is natural among mankind. Then Simeon said,
"Lord, now you let me depart from this life in peace, because my eyes have seen your Saviour."
The Saviour he spoke of is our Saviour Christ, who came to heal our wounds, which are our sins. Then Simeon said,
"whom you have prepared before the sight of all peoples." Not all people saw him bodily, but he is proclaimed to all people; let whoever will, believe.
Whoever believes in him sees him now through his faith, and in the eternal life with his own eyes. Simeon said further,
"He is a light for the revelation of the nations, and the glory of your people Israel." Simeon spoke all these words about the child to the heavenly Father, who sent him to mankind.
He is the true light that drove away the darkness of this life, as he himself said in his gospel,
"I am the light of the whole world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life."
Just as light drives away darkness, so too the love of Christ and faith in him drive all vices and sins away from our hearts; and he is the glory and bliss of all believing people.
Then Mary, the holy maiden, and the child's foster-father, Joseph, marvelled at the words that the old Simeon proclaimed about the child.

And Simeon then gave them a blessing, and prophesied still more about the child, and said, "This child is set for the fall of many people, and for the rising of many, and for a sign, and it will be spoken against."
Just as those who believe in Christ are saved through his coming, so also those who will not believe in Christ are doubly condemned.
They are guilty once through Adam's sin, and they are doubly condemned when they reject Christ's coming and will not believe in the true Savior.
To unbelieving people Christ came as a fall, and to the faithful as a rising; and also, to each believing person, Christ's coming was both a fall and a rising. How so?
He came so that he might overthrow every evil and raise up every good. Now he overthrows vices in us and raises up virtues. He overthrows pride and raises up humility.
He overthrows lust and raises up chastity. And he overthrows all vices in his chosen people, and raises up all goodness in them.
The good cannot be built unless the evil is first overthrown. "Christ came as a sign, and that sign is spoken against."
His birth is a wonderful sign, because he was born of a virgin, as no other is; and the unbelieving people spoke against that, and would not believe.
And also his resurrection from death, and his ascension to heaven, and all the wonders that he worked, all of them were signs, and the unbelieving spoke against them, and the believing believed.
Then the aged Simeon said to the blessed Mary, "His sword shall pass through your soul."
That sword signified Christ's passion. The blessed Mary was not slain or martyred in body, but in spirit;
When she saw her child taken, and iron nails driven through his hands and through his feet, and afterwards his side wounded with a spear, then Christ's suffering was her suffering;
and she was more than a martyr, because the suffering of her mind was greater than that of her body would have been, had she been martyred.
Simeon did not say that Christ's sword would pass through Mary's body, but through her soul. Christ's sword is set here, as we have said, for his passion.
Although Mary believed that Christ would rise from death, nevertheless her child's suffering went very sharply into her heart.
When Simeon had prophesied this prophecy about Christ, there came a certain widow, who was called Anna.
"She lived with her husband seven years, and afterwards she was a widow for eighty-four years, and served God with fasts, and with prayers, and in chastity;
and she was dwelling within God's temple during all that time; and she then came to the child, and prophesied about him, and gave praise to God."
Rightly was so holy a woman worthy to prophesy about Christ, since she had served God in chastity for so long.

Consider, you women, and understand what is written about her. She lived seven years with her husband, and after that she remained in the state of widowhood up to eighty-four years, living just as the apostle taught.
He said, the apostle Paul: "The widow who lives in luxuries is not living, but is dead."
This Anna, of whom we are speaking, did not love delicacies, but loved fasts. She did not love idle talk, but devoted herself to her prayers.
She did not go wandering about the land, but remained patiently within God's temple. If it should happen to a woman that she loses her husband, then let her take an example from this widow.
There are three states of life that bore witness concerning Christ; that is, virginity, widowhood, and lawful marriage.
A virgin is Christ's mother, and John the Baptist, who bore witness concerning Christ, lived in virginity, and many others besides him.
This Anna, of whom we spoke a while ago, was a widow. Zacharias, John's father, was a married man; both he and his wife prophesied about Christ.
These three states are pleasing to God, if they live rightly. Virginity exists both in men and in women.
Those have true virginity who from childhood remain in chastity, and through God's help scorn all lust in themselves, both of mind and of body.

These then have a hundredfold reward from God in the eternal life. Widows are those who, after the death of their spouses, live in chastity for the love of God: they then have a sixtyfold reward from God for their toil.
Those who rightly keep their marriage, and have intercourse at permitted times for the begetting of children, have a thirtyfold reward for their discretion.
He who wishes to fulfil his lust as often as he pleases is then compared to beasts and not to men.
Concerning this the apostle Paul taught, "Let those who have wives be as though they had none;"
for they must make amends for all their unlawful desires, either willingly in this life, or unwillingly after this life; and they will afterwards come to the eternal life with greater hardship.

Those who live outside lawful marriage, and run from one partner to another, have no share and no blessing with Christ unless they give it up and make amends for it. Let us now take up the gospel again where we left it before.
The blessed Mary and Joseph, the child's foster-father, returned with the child to the town of Nazareth;
"and the child grew and was strengthened and filled with wisdom, and the grace of God remained upon him."
He grew and was strengthened in his human nature, and he needed no growth and no strengthening in his divine nature.
He ate and drank and slept and grew in years, and yet his whole life was without sin. He would not have seemed a man if he had not lived a man's life.
He was filled with wisdom because he is himself wisdom, and in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead: bodily, God's grace dwelt in him.
It was a great grace to that human nature that he was the Son of God and God himself as soon as he began to be a man.
He was always God, begotten of the Father, and dwelling with the Father and with the Holy Spirit: those three are one God, indivisible;
three in persons, and one God in one Godhead, and dwelling forever in one nature. The Son alone took on human nature, and he who always was had a beginning.
He was a child and grew in his human nature, and willingly suffered death, and rose from death with the body in which he had suffered before,
and ascended to heaven, and now dwells forever in divine nature and in human nature, one Christ, both God and man, immortal, who before his passion was mortal.
He suffered, but from now on he will never suffer again; he will be forever, without end, just as eternal in his human nature as he is in his divine nature.
Let everyone also know that it is established in the customs of the Church that on this day we should carry our lights to church and have them blessed there,

and afterwards we should go with the lights among God's houses and sing the hymn that is appointed for it. Even if some people do not know how to sing, they should still carry the light in their hands;
because on this day the true Light, Christ, was brought to the temple, he who redeemed us from darkness and brings us to the eternal light, who lives and reigns forever without end. Amen.
